items: The 49th ASEAN Summit resulted in over a hundred outcome documents but failed to resolve ongoing issues such as the civil war in Myanmar and the South China Sea Code of Conduct negotiations.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. declared the summit a success, highlighting milestones like the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement and advancements in maritime cooperation.

MANILA, Philippines – After three days of summits and a seemingly endless procession of meetings, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) had over a hundred outcome documents to show for its time in Manila.
Yet it also had a civil war in Myanmar with no end in sight and a South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC) that, despite two decades of negotiations, its members and China still could not agree on.
Such was the record of the Philippines’ ASEAN chairmanship, which President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. declared a “success” on Tuesday, November 17, as he formally handed over the reins to Singapore.

“I would say that it was a success simply because of the work that we were able to achieve. The one thing I did not want to do was to waste an opportunity such as this by just doing this hosting,” Marcos told the media following the summit’s closing ceremony.

The 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits brought leaders to the Philippines in a world beset by overlapping crises. Ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine have thrown global energy and food supplies into disarray, El Niño threatens agricultural production, and economies across the region are reeling from rising costs and varying levels of domestic unrest. (READ: Marcos gov’t on track to miss growth target for fourth straight year)

Against this backdrop, Southeast Asian leaders and their allies had much to discuss across the different meetings that Manila has played host to. Read Rappler’s live updates for more details on the key developments.

To be fair, there were milestones. ASEAN signed its Digital Economy Framework Agreement, establishing common rules for digital trade and payments. All 11 members also signed an enhanced memorandum of understanding on the ASEAN Power Grid, with Marcos announcing that a proposed undersea cable would connect Sabah to Mindanao. The bloc also advanced initiatives on maritime cooperation, disaster response, online scams, and child protection.
But what of ASEAN’s most difficult problems?

blocks.caption: Rappler Recap: PH ends ASEAN chairship with gains, but Myanmar and COC unresolved

blocks.text: Top on Marcos’ plate was Myanmar, still embroiled in a political crisis that has seen it sidelined from ASEAN since the military-backed government seized power in 2021.
Marcos said Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, serving as ASEAN’s special envoy, had focused on facilitating dialogue and expanding humanitarian assistance.
“None of those items are easy. However, the one that is easily understandable and immediately implementable is the assistance on the humanitarian side,” Marcos told the media on Tuesday.

ASEAN leaders agreed to pursue a “calibrated, progress-based approach” toward Myanmar, leaving open the possibility of gradually restoring its full political representation if the country demonstrates concrete progress under ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus. In their review of the Myanmar situation, the leaders also reiterated their “deep concern over the insufficient progress in the implementation of the 5PC.”
But until progress towards peace comes, Myanmar remains barred from having its political leaders join the high-stakes ASEAN summits and foreign ministers’ meetings.
“The ball is very much now in the court of Myanmar and its present leadership,” Marcos said.

blocks.caption: Rappler Recap: Trump meets ASEAN leaders at special summit

blocks.text: It would also have been a perfect win to conclude COC negotiations during Marcos’ year at the helm of ASEAN. Instead, that too failed to live up to ambitions.
The President told reporters that 85% to 90% of the agreement had been completed — a more optimistic assessment than his foreign secretary’s earlier estimate of around 80%.
According to Marcos, much of the remaining work revolves around the definition of terms.

“There are definitions, there are phrases, and there are paragraphs that need to be clearly defined so that it is very understandable and very clear to everyone involved that these are the rules,” he said.

But absent from his remarks was perhaps the most contentious issue of all: whether the eventual COC would be legally binding. This is particularly important for the Philippines, given its continuing confrontations with China in the West Philippine Sea.

In the meantime, Marcos said ASEAN and China had reached a “tacit agreement” to continue abiding by the 2002 Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea, the earlier, nonbinding framework that the COC is meant to build upon.

blocks.caption: Sorry, Marcos can’t keep his ‘very, very important guest’ waiting

blocks.text: Although the ASEAN closing ceremony was already over, leaders were asked to stretch their stay a little longer for one final meeting, a special summit with visiting US President Donald Trump.

Perhaps that was why Marcos was also mum on the controversial US-led Pax Silica initiative, which has drawn protests across the metro and in the provinces. Officials had already previously said no major announcement on the initiative was planned during the summit.
Unfortunately, there was little opportunity to press the Philippine leader further.
His final briefing allowed questions from just one pre-selected reporter before he was whisked away to meet a particularly important guest. Marcos, it seemed, had kept that guest waiting long enough.
“I can’t keep the president of the United States waiting, so I have to go. I’m sorry,” he told reporters on his way out.
And with that, Marcos was off to meet Trump, leaving Singapore, ASEAN’s 2027 chair, to inherit some very old problems to deal with. – Rappler.com
